 Cantor: Will the most expensive Halloween ever become the grinch that stole Christmas?
 Opinion 
 Cantor: Will the most expensive Halloween ever become the grinch that stole Christmas?
 Martin Cantor 
 // October 22, 2026 
 // 
 Listen to this article 
 MARTIN CANTOR: Open space purchases have really cost $8.2 billion in lost economic activity. 
 The Blueprint:
 Halloween costume costs up 200% due to tariffs and inflation
 Candy prices rise 8.1%, sugar up 16%, cocoa affected by West Africa drought
 Long Island inflation increased 4.5% since September 2025
 Credit card debt rises with average balance at $8,000 and 21.16% interest
 Dressed as a twin-headed ghoul, inflation and tariffs are about to make the upcoming Halloween holiday the most expensive ever. And if the cost of Halloween is not scary enough, the upcoming holiday travel and shopping season may not be merry for Long Island retailers and travelers as tariffs and inflation shrink discretionary income.
 The cost of Halloween costumes, averaging $60, are over 200% more than they were in 2024 due to tariffs on imported plastics, textiles and materials, and higher manufacturing and transportation costs. Your favorite candy costs 8.1% more, sugar costs have increased by 16%, and that chocolate you crave is more expensive due to drought and heat in West Africa causing cocoa prices to increase. Additionally, pumpkin picking season began with a nightmare, with rain not only taking away five pumpkin-picking Sundays, but combined with extreme heat pumpkin crops rotted on the vine, causing pumpkin price increases at farm stands and pumpkin fields. Thus, according to the National Retail Federation, expected Halloween spending of discretionary income will average $115.14 per person or between $159 to $296 per household. And, after the candy is eaten or given to trick-or-treaters, and the costumes are put away for another year, attention turns to the holiday vacation and shopping season. Or does it?
 With discretionary income spent on Halloween, and with Long Island inflation increasing by 4.5% since September 2025—led by motor fuel increasing by 37%, gasoline by 36.9% and energy by 21.5% further shrinking discretionary income—the federal reserve’s latest Survey of Consumer Finances (SCF) indicates that holiday revelers may be travelling less this year. 
 The SCF reported that vacation expenditures capture a more discretionary form of spending that varies across families. While median vacation spending was $1,000 per family, 39% of families—primarily younger families, families with limited income and wealth and those with health issues—spent nothing on vacations during 2025. With vacation spending consistent with luxury spending of discretionary income, less vacation spending can also be viewed as an indicator of financial vulnerability that may impact the holiday shopping season if not for credit card spending, which in 2025 reached a record $1.2 trillion. The question is how much longer or how much more can consumers rely on credit cards to fuel their holiday spending?
 Clearly credit card use has increased, and with it came an increase in the financial vulnerability of consumer households. When 45% of families with an average balance on their credit cards after their last payment increased to $8,000, the financial stress is evident considering the average credit card interest rate is 21.16%. This further drains discretionary income, worsening the total debt-to-income ratio, which increased to 94.9% in 2025 from 89.4% in 2022. Also increasing the debt payments-to-income ratio by 33% for the 8.6% of families with debt-payments-to income ratio of greater than 40%, the most since 2013.
 American families are struggling with economic triage. That is having to choose what is more critical to buy and what loans are more critical to pay. Their propensity to stay current with debt payments worsened in 2025: Families falling behind in loan payments increased nearly 67% between 12% in 2022 to 20% in 2025. 
 Should the economic struggles continue, the twin ghouls of Halloween—inflation and tariffs—will morph into the grinches who stole the holiday shopping season.
 Martin Cantor is director of the Long Island Center for Socio-Economic Policy and a former Suffolk County economic development commissioner. He can be reached at  [email protected] .
